profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab after a reproduction effort on a paper about squared-loss training instability in expressive neural and nonlinear conic approximation models produced inconsistent results across two internal runs. The team is trying to diagnose why one reproduction notebook shows abrupt changes in fitted parameters and extra bad local minima when a single label is perturbed by 1e-3, while the other internal report shows only mild variation and no clearly isolated spurious basin. The agenda is to compare what each person means by the observed 'instability,' identify the likely source of the discrepancy in their reproduction pipeline, and agree on a concrete debugging plan for rerunning the sensitivity experiment. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for a revised rerun, but not yet a final scientific conclusion.

members.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
members.expertise: optimization theory for neural networks, loss landscapes, reproducibility analysis
members.background: Lena leads the lab's theory-to-experiment validation work and often converts formal claims about instability and local minima into compact numerical demonstrations using small synthetic datasets.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the paper's core theoretical framing and is worried that the current failed reproduction may simply be due to an implementation mismatch rather than a genuine problem with the claim; she also wants a quick resolution before an internal reading group presentation.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the paper's 'instability,' the relevant object is the discontinuous change in the argmin set or fitted parameters under infinitesimal label perturbations, not merely prediction drift.

A 'small label perturbation' experiment is naturally done by holding the optimization trajectory as comparable as possible across runs, including the same initialization and same continuation path over perturbed labels.
The 'regularized run' is just a diagnostic control with a tiny weight penalty added on top of the original squared-loss setup, so it should still be interpreted as the same instability experiment.

Referring to 'the two-layer variable-width network result' still includes width changes that happen through effectively inactive units retained in the parameterization rather than physically changing tensor shapes.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: PyTorch experiment pipelines, hyperparameter sweeps, numerical diagnostics
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's training and evaluation stack and translated the paper's abstract claims into automated scripts that compare optimization outcomes across seeds, perturbations, and architecture settings.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid over-attributing discrepancies to deep theoretical phenomena when they may just reflect brittle toy setups, and he is concerned that any debugging fix should generalize to the pipeline rather than becoming a one-off handcrafted reproduction.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing 'instability,' the operationally meaningful quantity is whether predictions or final training loss change sharply across reruns, since parameter values can move a lot without changing the fitted function.

A 'small label perturbation' experiment should sample optimization afresh for each perturbed dataset, including a new random seed, because that reflects the practical training problem rather than a path-following continuation study.
A 'regularized run' means the experiment has become a different training objective whose behavior should be evaluated on its own terms, not merely as a light-touch control of the original claim.
Referring to the 'variable-width network' means actually retraining explicit models at widths 4, 8, and 16, not keeping a wider model and letting some units collapse to near-zero.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they are checking whether the training problem is 'unstable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means instability of the solution set: tiny label changes causing discontinuous jumps in minimizers or fitted parameter configurations, even if training loss stays low.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means unstable empirical behavior: materially different predictions, losses, or convergence outcomes across nearby runs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research conversation, 'instability' is a familiar umbrella term, and both definitions are reasonable in context; because they are troubleshooting a reproduction rather than debating theory, each assumes the other's usage is close enough.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to rerun the 'small perturbation' sensitivity check.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a continuation-style experiment: perturb one label by 1e-3 while keeping initialization, optimizer state convention, and run pairing matched so observed changes can be attributed to the label perturbation itself.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes independent reruns per perturbed dataset: regenerate the seed and launch the standard training job for each label variant, because that is the lab's default way to assess robustness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both procedures sound like standard ways to 'rerun the perturbation experiment,' and neither person expects the other to spell out seed-handling in a short troubleshooting meeting because experiment scripts usually encode that implicitly.

misalignment_points.topic: What the regularized comparison is supposed to show
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the 'regularized check' as evidence about whether regularization fixes the issue.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the check succeeds if adding a tiny parameter norm penalty still leaves the same qualitative discontinuity and spurious basin phenomenon, matching the paper's claim that regularization does not generally remove it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the check succeeds if regularization makes optimization behavior smoother in practice, such as fewer bad runs or less variation across seeds, even if the exact pathological structure is not exhaustively preserved.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are cooperatively asking whether regularization 'helps,' but one is using a theory-faithful falsification standard and the other a practical stabilization standard; the phrase 'fixes the issue' sounds shared while hiding different pass/fail criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: Which variable-width setup they are talking about
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both mention reproducing the 'variable-width network case.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the notebook where a width-16 model is trained with some units becoming effectively inactive, treating this as a variable-width realization within a single parameterization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the sweep job that trains separate explicit architectures of widths 4, 8, and 16 and compares their landscapes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both objects legitimately fall under the paper's broad variable-width language, and each has recently worked on only one of them, so the shared shorthand feels unambiguous in the moment.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor this quickly. In the notebook, a 1e-3 change to one label made the optimizer track into a different minimizer in the width-16 parameterization with several units effectively inactive. That is exactly the instability the paper is about. If Arjun's pipeline missed it, it's probably because the implementation isn't matching the intended setup, and I really need a clean story before the reading group.
turns.utterance: I think the mismatch matters because the instability should be pretty visible even when we only nudge one label by 1e-3 in the variable-width network case. That's why the two internal results feel too far apart to just shrug off.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, the practical signs just weren't dramatic. Across the reruns, loss stayed about the same and predictions barely moved, so calling it unstable feels overstated unless we're seeing something that matters functionally. I don't want us to chase a toy artifact if the deployed behavior is basically unchanged.
turns.utterance: Right, but in my runs the training loss was basically the same and the predictions only shifted a little, so I wasn't seeing the same instability signal you were expecting.

turns.inner_thought: He's focusing on outputs. But the whole point is that nearby labels can send you to a different basin or branch of minimizers while still fitting well. The fitted parameters and basin structure are the issue, not whether the function values wiggle much on this tiny dataset.
turns.utterance: For me, the key symptom is that the optimizer can land somewhere qualitatively different after that tiny perturbation, even if both fits still look numerically fine.

turns.inner_thought: I should explain the pipeline choice plainly. I used the standard launcher: every perturbed dataset is its own job, new seed, same config template. That's how we normally assess sensitivity, and I don't want to special-case one paper unless we have to.
turns.utterance: On the small perturbation check, I just reused the standard sweep launcher, so each perturbed dataset trained as a fresh run with its own seed.

turns.inner_thought: Ah, that could absolutely wash it out. If the initialization and run pairing aren't matched, then ordinary optimizer randomness gets mixed in with the label perturbation. For this experiment, the whole point is to isolate the effect of the 1e-3 nudge along a comparable training path.
turns.utterance: Got it. I had expected the small perturbation check to keep the two runs closely paired, so the label change rather than ordinary training noise would account for the jump.

turns.inner_thought: I should mention the regularized version too, because that made the behavior look a lot less brittle in practice. To me that means regularization may already be solving most of the problem, or at least making it less concerning operationally.
turns.utterance: I also included the regularized check, and there the bad behavior looked much less severe, which is part of why I thought the issue was mostly mitigated.

turns.inner_thought: I need to gently recenter what that check is for. A tiny weight penalty was only supposed to be a diagnostic control layered onto the same squared-loss setup, not a new criterion where any smoother behavior counts as success. The claim survives if the same discontinuity story is still there.
turns.utterance: For me, the regularized check was mainly there to test whether regularization actually fixes the issue, not just whether it makes things look calmer at a glance.

turns.inner_thought: This may be another source of drift: I ran the regularized jobs on the explicit width sweep, 4, 8, and 16, because that's what I took the variable-width network case to mean. If Lena was looking at some other setup, that would explain a lot of the mismatch.
turns.utterance: That may also connect to the setup I used: my regularized runs were on the variable-width network case in the width sweep, with 4, 8, and 16 hidden units, because I assumed that was the relevant version.

turns.inner_thought: There it is. I've been using the notebook with one wider model where several units go effectively inactive and still calling that the variable-width case. No wonder we're talking past each other while thinking we're aligned.
turns.utterance: Ah, okay. The discrepant notebook on my side used a single wider model where some units effectively turned off, and I had been referring to that as the variable-width network case too.

turns.inner_thought: Best path forward is to reproduce her exact configuration inside the pipeline and log everything side by side. I'll still want predictions and losses, but I can add parameter traces and whatever basin/minimum labeling we have so we can compare both views without handwaving.
